Assignment 6 Text Mining

Title: Exploring Joyful Language in Jane Austen’s Emma using Tidytext

Instructions

Complete the following exercises using the appropriate packages in R. Ensure that your solutions are optimized and use functional programming principles where applicable.

  1. Load the necessary libraries.
  2. Answer each question in separate R code chunks.
  3. Provide detailed explanations for your approach.
  4. Submit the rendered HTML file.

Objective:

Use the tidytext package and three different sentiment lexicons (nrc, afinn, bing) to explore positive/joyful words in Emma by Jane Austen. You will tokenize the text, apply sentiment filters, visualize frequent sentiment words using ggplot2, and create a word cloud.

Tasks:

  1. Data Preparation

    • Load the austen_books() dataset from the janeaustenr package.
    books <- austen_books()
head(books)
    # A tibble: 6 × 2
  text                    book               
  <chr>                   <fct>              
1 "SENSE AND SENSIBILITY" Sense & Sensibility
2 ""                      Sense & Sensibility
3 "by Jane Austen"        Sense & Sensibility
4 ""                      Sense & Sensibility
5 "(1811)"                Sense & Sensibility
6 ""                      Sense & Sensibility
    • Group by book and detect chapter boundaries using regex.
    library(stringr)
original_books <- austen_books() |>
  group_by(book)
head(original_books)
    # A tibble: 6 × 2
# Groups:   book [1]
  text                    book               
  <chr>                   <fct>              
1 "SENSE AND SENSIBILITY" Sense & Sensibility
2 ""                      Sense & Sensibility
3 "by Jane Austen"        Sense & Sensibility
4 ""                      Sense & Sensibility
5 "(1811)"                Sense & Sensibility
6 ""                      Sense & Sensibility
    • Create linenumber and chapter columns.
    grouped_books <- austen_books()|>
  mutate(
    line_number = row_number(),
    chapter = cumsum(str_detect(text, regex("^chapter [\\divxlc]", 
                                            ignore_case = TRUE)))
  ) |>
ungroup()

    • What: Loaded austen_books() (a function, not a dataset, so called it directly), grouped by book, and created linenumber and chapter.

    • Why: Grouping makes line numbers and chapter counts restart for each novel. The regex ^chapter [\\divxlc] finds headings in both numeric and Roman numeral styles, and cumsum() turns those heading locations into a running chapter number. ungroup() prevents later steps from accidentally running per book.

  2. Tokenization

    • Use unnest_tokens() to tokenize text into individual words.
    tidy_books <- original_books |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text)
head(tidy_books)
    # A tibble: 6 × 2
# Groups:   book [1]
  book                word       
  <fct>               <chr>      
1 Sense & Sensibility sense      
2 Sense & Sensibility and        
3 Sense & Sensibility sensibility
4 Sense & Sensibility by         
5 Sense & Sensibility jane       
6 Sense & Sensibility austen

    • What: Used unnest_tokens(word, text) to split each line into one word per row.

    • Why: The tidy format (one token per row) lets you use dplyr verbs like join and count. It also lowercases and strips punctuation, so “Emma,” and “emma” count as the same word.

  3. Sentiment Analysis

    • Filter joy/positive words from each of the three sentiment lexicons:

      • nrc (joy)
      • afinn (positive scores ≥ 1)
      • bing (positive)
    library(textdata)
library(dplyr)
nrc_joy <- get_sentiments("nrc") |>
  filter(sentiment == "joy")

afinn_positive <- get_sentiments("afinn") |>
  filter(value >= 1) 

bing_positive <- get_sentiments("bing") |>
  filter(sentiment == "positive")

nrow(nrc_joy)
    [1] 687
    nrow(afinn_positive)
    [1] 878
    nrow(bing_positive)
    [1] 2005

    • What: Filtered joy words from nrc, positive scores (value >= 1) from afinn, and positive words from bing.

    • Why: Each lexicon is structured differently: NRC has emotion categories, AFINN has numeric scores, and Bing has binary labels. So each needs a different filter to define “positive.” You can also note that this means the three lists differ in size and coverage.

    • Join each with Emma’s text and:

      • Count word frequency.
      • Filter for frequently occurring words (n > 50).
      • Visualize using a bar chart (ggplot2) and a word cloud (wordcloud).
    library(wordcloud)
    Loading required package: RColorBrewer
    emma <- tidy_books |>
  filter(book == "Emma")

emma_nrc <- emma |>
  inner_join(nrc_joy, by = "word") |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  filter(n > 50)

emma_afinn <- emma |>
  inner_join(afinn_positive, by = "word") |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  filter(n > 50)

emma_bing <- emma |>
  inner_join(bing_positive, by = "word") |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  filter(n > 50)

    • What: Used inner_join() to keep only Emma words found in each lexicon, then count() and filter(n > 50).

    • Why: An inner join drops words with no sentiment label. The n > 50 threshold focuses on the words that actually shape the book’s tone rather than rare one-offs.

    plot_bar <- function(df, title) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x = reorder(word, n), y = n)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(title = title, x = "Word", y = "Count")
}

plot_cloud <- function(df, title) {
  set.seed(123)
  wordcloud(words = df$word, freq = df$n, min.freq = 1,
            random.order = FALSE, colors = brewer.pal(8, "Dark2"))
  title(title)
}

plot_bar(emma_nrc, "Frequent NRC Joy Words in Emma")
    plot_bar(emma_afinn, "Frequent AFINN Positive Words in Emma")
    plot_bar(emma_bing, "Frequent Bing Positive Words in Emma")
    plot_cloud(emma_nrc, "NRC Joy Words in Emma")
    plot_cloud(emma_afinn, "AFINN Positive Words in Emma")
    plot_cloud(emma_bing, "Bing Positive Words in Emma")

    • What: A bar chart and word cloud per lexicon.

    • Why: Bar charts show exact counts and make ranking easy. Word clouds give a quick visual impression of relative frequency, but are less precise. Using both gives precision and overview.
